claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §4.2.1: "If the port subcomponent is empty or not given, TCP port 80 (the reserved port for WWW services) is the default." §4.2.2: "If the port subcomponent is empty or not given, TCP port 443 (the reserved port for HTTP over TLS) is the default." Both grepped verbatim in the local mirror.

RFC 9110 §4.3.3: the registered name "is an indirect identifier for use with a name resolution service, such as DNS, to find an address for an appropriate origin server"; and "a client MAY attempt access by resolving the host identifier to an IP address, establishing a TCP connection to that address on the indicated port, and sending over that connection an HTTP request message". Resolution precedes the connection.

RFC 9110 §4.2.1: the "http" scheme identifies "a potential HTTP origin server listening for TCP ([TCP]) connections on a given port". §4.3.3: "establishing a TCP connection to that address on the indicated port, and sending over that connection an HTTP request message". RFC 9112 §9.1 (HTTP/1.1): "Each HTTP connection maps to one underlying transport connection." The connection exists before the request is sent over it.

RFC 9112 §9.7 TLS Connection Initiation: "The HTTP client also acts as the TLS client. It initiates a connection to the server on the appropriate port and sends the TLS ClientHello to begin the TLS handshake. When the TLS handshake has finished, the client may then initiate the first HTTP request." RFC 9110 §4.3.3 for https gives the same order: resolve, "establishing a TCP connection", "securing the connection end-to-end by successfully initiating TLS over TCP", then sending the request.

RFC 9110 §7.1: "To perform an action on a 'target resource', the client sends a request message containing enough components of its parsed target URI" — one request, one target. RFC 9112 §9.2: "More than one response message per request only occurs when one or more informational responses (1xx) precede a final response to the same request." So a second file needs a second request/response pair.

RFC 9112 §4 Status Line: "The first line of a response message is the status-line, consisting of the protocol version, a space (SP), the status code, and another space and ending with an OPTIONAL textual phrase describing the status code." RFC 9112 is the HTTP/1.1 message syntax, which is the version the claim names, and the captured run's first line is "HTTP/1.1 200 OK".

No permitted source covers browser subresource fetching. The HTML Living Standard is not a docs root in content/versions.yaml and is not mirrored under refs/ (refs/ holds only rfc/, dotnet-docs, aspnetcore-docs, docker-docs, kubernetes-website, flutter-website). Grepped refs/rfc for embedded/hyperlink fetching: nothing. curl and docker could not be run in this session, so the lab could not be started to observe a browser either.

No permitted source. TCP has no key in content/versions.yaml, RFC 9293 is not mirrored (refs/rfc holds 6265, 9110, 9111, 9112 only), and the mirrored RFCs say nothing about RST-on-closed-port or connect() error codes. Attempted to settle it by execution (curl/nc against a closed port); command execution was refused in this session. Kind is behavior, so this does not block approval, but nothing in the lesson's own sources supports it.

RFC 9110 §4.3.4 does not say the exchange is aborted: "If the certificate is not valid for the target URI's origin, a user agent MUST either obtain confirmation from the user before proceeding (see Section 3.5) or terminate the connection with a bad certificate error." A browser may therefore continue after the user clicks through — which is exactly what stage-0 produces, since the Caddyfile uses `tls internal` (a certificate Caddy signs itself). The ordering half of the claim holds (RFC 9112 §9.7).
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: …and a certificate the client does not trust stops the exchange after the TCP connection is open and before any HTTP request is sent, unless the user chooses to continue past the browser's warning.

claim_verdicts.evidence: STAGE.md at stage-0: "HTTPS is on `https://donhang.local:8443` with a certificate Caddy signs itself; add `127.0.0.1 donhang.local` to your hosts file to open it in a browser." scripts/up.sh:13 prints the same instruction. Caddyfile has `:8080 {` for the plain site and `donhang.local:8443 {` for TLS. docker-compose.yml gives the lab box `extra_hosts: donhang.local:127.0.0.1`, which is why the script resolves that name inside the box but the host machine does not.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang STAGE.md:15-17, scripts/up.sh:12-13, Caddyfile:11 and 95, docker-compose.yml:27-28

claim_verdicts.evidence: The committed CI capture contains, in order: "Name:\tlab", "Address: 172.28.0.12", "   connected to port 8080", "    Protocol  : TLSv1.3", "HTTP/1.1 200 OK", and three lines "   200 http://localhost:8080/{index,login,cached}.html". The script's line 5 is `[ -f /.dockerenv ] || exec "$(dirname "$0")/../lab-run.sh" "$0" "$@"`, which is the re-run inside the lab box. The lesson's output block matches that file with the header block collapsed to `...` (A.6).

Settled by the recorded run of that exact command line. Step 4 of the capture prints only the header block — HTTP/1.1 200 OK, Accept-Ranges, Content-Length: 350, Content-Type, Etag, Last-Modified, Server: Caddy, Vary, Date — and no HTML, even though Content-Length reports a 350-byte body (= the byte size of www/index.html). So `-D -` wrote headers to stdout and `-o /dev/null` discarded the body. Step 5 prints exactly "   200 <url>" per exchange, matching the -w format string. curl's manual was not used: curl has no key in versions.yaml.

`tools/extract-code www/index.html --tag stage-0` returns 17 lines containing exactly three anchors — href="/login.html", href="/cached.html", href="/redirect" — and no img, link or script element; head holds only meta charset and title. The lesson's html block reproduces lines 1-16 character-for-character after whitespace normalisation. www/ at stage-0 holds only cached.html, index.html and login.html.

The first clause is settled by the repository (see claim 13): index.html embeds nothing, so this HTML asks for no further file. The rest — "fetched only if the reader clicks them" and "any extra row the browser adds on its own" — is browser behaviour with no permitted source, the same limit as claim 7. Note the claim's own hedge about extra rows never reached the lesson: see the Try it issue below.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang/www/index.html at stage-0; refs/ listing; content/versions.yaml

claim_verdicts.suggested_text: The wording differs between browsers, but the failure falls into one of a few categories — name, connection, certificate, server — and that category usually tells you which step to look at first.

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §4.2.1: "http-URI = "http" "://" authority path-abempty [ "?" query ]", and "The origin server for an "http" URI is identified by the authority component, which includes a host identifier … and optional port number". The path follows the whole authority — host AND port — not the host. Every address in this lesson writes a port, so "the part after the host" reads as ":8080/index.html". Same finding as the previous round; the lesson text is unchanged.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: Claim 16 should read "…then a path; the path is the part after the authority, that is after the host and any port". Section 4 should read "naming one path: the part of the address after the host and port, such as `/index.html`".

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §4.3.3 (https): a client "MAY attempt access by resolving the host identifier to an IP address, establishing a TCP connection to that address on the indicated port, securing the connection end-to-end by successfully initiating TLS over TCP …, and sending over that connection an HTTP request message". RFC 9112 §9.7: "When the TLS handshake has finished, the client may then initiate the first HTTP request." The request naming the page is sent only after all three steps.

RFC 9110 §15.3.1: "The 200 (OK) status code indicates that the request has succeeded." It rides on the status line (RFC 9112 §4, claim 6). Consistent with the CI capture, whose step 4 first line is "HTTP/1.1 200 OK" and whose step 5 prints 200 for all three addresses.

The colon clause is right: steps 3-5 are each handed a name and a port with no preceding connect step, so each resolves and connects itself (RFC 9110 §4.3.3; RFC 9112 §9.7 for s_client). The opening clause "also performs the earlier steps of the chain" is not: steps 4 and 5 use `http://localhost:8080`, so they never perform step 3, the encryption step — the script's own step-3 echo says "(only on the HTTPS port)". The lesson repeats the over-broad form; see the section 5 issue.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: In the script, openssl s_client and curl each resolve the name and open their own connection before doing the step their echo names; the encryption step happens only on the HTTPS port, so the curl commands in steps 4 and 5 never run it.

issues.text: "The later commands still run the earlier steps silently" is false for the encryption step and contradicts the line directly above it. Steps 4 and 5 curl `http://localhost:8080/...`, so no TLS handshake ever happens there; the script's own step-3 echo says "(only on the HTTPS port)". A reader who takes this sentence at face value concludes that plain HTTP also agrees on encryption. Claim 19 is narrower than the lesson: it only says the commands resolve the name and open their own connection.
issues.quote: The later commands still run the earlier steps silently.
issues.fix: Replace with: "Each later command still resolves the name and opens its own connection before doing its own step; only the HTTPS port runs the encryption step, which is why step 3 uses a different address." Update claim 19's text the same way.
